claims.text: The strength and deformation behavior of multi-component concentrated alloys are governed by the degree of lattice distortion and localized chemical heterogeneity.
The relevant initial materials are as-cast, single-phase concentrated alloys.
The alloys contain multiple principal elements with a uniform overall composition.
Changing elemental concentrations and cooling rates can vary lattice distortion and local chemical clustering while phase structure remains constant.
Lattice distortions act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Local chemical clusters act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Enhanced lattice distortion creates local stress fields and obstacles that hinder dislocation movement.
Chemical heterogeneity creates local stress fields and obstacles that hinder dislocation movement.
Hindering dislocation motion increases yield strength.
Lattice distortion and chemical heterogeneity alter failure behavior through localized accumulation of plastic strain.
Beyond a critical level, excessive distortion may cause strain localization.
Distortion-induced strain localization may cause premature failure.
Relative to binary or less-complex alloys, concentrated alloys with optimized lattice distortion and chemical heterogeneity will have higher yield strength.
Optimized lattice distortion and chemical heterogeneity will produce a controllable deformation process.
A lack of lattice distortion and local chemical heterogeneity will result in lower strength and different failure mechanisms.
The proposed mechanism applies when the alloys remain single-phase and secondary phases or intermetallic compounds are suppressed.
